summary:
Entry screening at United Arab Emirates airports tests a traveller's appearance against the sex recorded in the passport. In 2025 two Israeli transgender women were held for several hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to establish whether their genital anatomy matched the female marker in their passports, mocked by staff, refused entry and had their passports confiscated.

Earlier refusals follow the same pattern. In March 2022 the Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, questioned for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of an Expo 2020 appearance because her passport recorded male sex. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport and her passport confiscated after officials declined to treat her gender as valid. In May 2025 the Armenian transgender rights defender Lilit Martirosyan was detained while transiting Dubai and told she could not enter the country as a transgender person before being allowed to leave.

Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, in force since 2 January 2022, carries the offence most often used against gender expression. Article 412(2) punishes a man who disguises himself as a woman to enter a space reserved for women with up to one year in prison and a fine of up to AED 10,000. It replaced the broader Article 359 of the 1987 penal code, which prohibited clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances. Legal reviews of the UAE record that the criminal law penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles and that unconventional appearance routinely produces arrest, confinement or expulsion.

The most fully documented prosecution of visitors is that of the Singaporean transgender woman Nur Qistina Fitriah Ibrahim and her companion Muhammed Fadli Abdul Rahman. They arrived in Abu Dhabi on 8 August 2017 and were arrested the next day in a mixed-gender shopping mall, wearing jeans, sneakers and long-sleeved shirts, for looking feminine. They were charged under Article 359 and under a local public morals provision carrying up to two years and AED 15,000. On 20 August 2017 they were sentenced to one year each without legal representation. They spent nearly three weeks in custody, part of it in a cell designated for effeminate detainees, where guards shaved their heads and discarded Ibrahim's hormone pills. The sentences were converted to deportation and a fine on 27 August and they were deported the following day. Other transgender women and feminine-appearing people were held in the same facility solely for looking feminine in mixed-gender public places.

Arrests for dress and appearance recur. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women in Dubai who called police to report prejudice they had witnessed were themselves arrested for imitating women, held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. A June 2011 Dubai police campaign targeted transsexuals and boyat, further arrests for disguising as a woman were recorded in March, July and December 2012, and foreign residents were arrested and deported in 2020 for clothing deemed inappropriate for their sex. In 2005 Abu Dhabi police raided a hotel gathering and arrested 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding; twelve were convicted, eleven receiving five-year sentences and one a single year, with initial reports that some were offered hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences.

Article 409(1)(b) criminalises consensual same-sex relations with a minimum of six months' imprisonment and no prescribed maximum, and Article 409 also reaches unmarried different-sex couples. Under Article 409(5) a prosecution requires a complaint by a spouse or guardian, which may be withdrawn at any time; because civil guardianship ends at 18, the sources conclude that no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, while a father or male relative acting as wali, or a husband, can supply one where a woman is concerned. The 2020 amendments removed stoning and flogging, and the 2021 law does not provide the death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; capital punishment for sexual offences is confined to non-consensual acts such as rape of a minor or rape causing death, and no death sentence for homosexual activity is documented. United States State Department reporting records no known arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct since at least 2015, but public decency prosecutions continue: two Indian men received six months and deportation in 2012 for sex in a public bus-station toilet, a British man and another man received three years and deportation for drunken public sex the same year, a Belgian man received a year and deportation in June 2012 after admitting a relationship with a Filipino man, and police broke up a party of 30 men in Dubai on 21 March 2012.

No legal gender recognition exists. Sex reassignment surgery is confined to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances. No UAE law or policy prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. LGBTI organisations cannot register and none operates openly; Dubai has no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs, and a nightclub that hosted a dedicated LGBTQ night was shut down by the government. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, so a trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship has no partner recognition, and the relationship itself falls within Article 409.

Detention carries specific risk. Transgender detainees have been held in cells designated for effeminate people. Reports describe beatings and forced anal examinations amounting to torture following suspected or established same-sex conduct. Involuntary hormonal and psychological treatment has been administered, including in connection with suspected same-sex conduct, and no law or regulation prohibits or discourages conversion practices.

A Brazilian transgender woman was held in the UAE from September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and accused her consulate of negligence; the case is the clearest record of a trans foreign national in prolonged custody.

Official posture is openly hostile. Officials have stated publicly that there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 over a same-sex relationship and Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a transgender flag reading Protect Trans Lives. The sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word gay or sex, and Amazon blocked 150 search terms including lgbtq and pride on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties.
tangentialFactors:
Public decency provisions reach conduct that has nothing to do with gender identity. A Scottish tourist arrested in October 2017 for public indecency after touching a man's hip had the charges dropped following the intervention of Dubai's ruler, which shows that enforcement in this area is discretionary as well as criminal.

The same provisions can turn a complainant into a suspect. In July 2007 a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy kidnapped and raped in Dubai was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country; he was later awarded AED 15 million in civil compensation, and the family accused the authorities of failing to disclose that one of the assailants was HIV-positive. A visitor reporting a sexual assault cannot assume the complaint will be handled solely as a complaint.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, and surgical transition is available only within limited, state-regulated circumstances. No law or policy protects against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, in employment or any other field.

LGBTI organisations cannot register and none operates openly. Conversion practices are neither prohibited nor discouraged by any law or regulation, and involuntary hormonal and psychological treatment has been administered to people suspected of same-sex conduct.

Foreign residents are exposed on appearance grounds: arrests and deportations for clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex were recorded in 2020, and the 2017 Abu Dhabi case ended in deportation after a one-year sentence. Custody brings additional exposure, including cells designated for effeminate detainees, forced anal examinations and the removal of hormone medication.

For citizens, the Article 409(5) complaint requirement places the decision to prosecute in the hands of a spouse or a male guardian, so family members control the legal exposure of a trans relative.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 account of X-ray examination at Dubai airport rests on the testimony of the two travellers; no response from UAE authorities appears in the source inventory.

No UAE statistics on arrests or prosecutions for gender expression or same-sex conduct are published. The absence of recorded prosecutions since 2015 rests on diplomatic human-rights reporting rather than court records, and the practical operation of the Article 409(5) complaint requirement in recent years is not documented.

Whether Article 412(2) is applied outside women-only spaces is unresolved in the sources; the 2017 convictions used the predecessor Article 359 together with a local public morals provision. The outcome of the Brazilian national's custody is not recorded.

The reports that men detained after the 2005 Abu Dhabi raid were offered hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences are initial reports, not confirmed sentencing records.

No general homicide or violence data for the UAE appears in the inventory, so no trans-specific violence rate can be stated or compared against a background rate.
